source.title: Effect of age on response to amblyopia treatment in children

confidence_rationale: Human, randomized-trial-derived evidence for the combination ARC-075 prescribes: handicapping the dominant pathway lets the weaker pathway regain function, and it works best inside a developmental window (children under 7 responded more than 7-13 year olds). High source quality, but the mapping is by analogy -- ocular dominance is input competition in sensory cortex, not scorer competition in action selection -- and the graded, non-absolute age effect (some older children still respond) tempers any hard-closure reading.
failure_signatures: Children 7 to <13 years were significantly less responsive than younger groups for moderate and severe amblyopia, but some older children still showed a marked response, so the window is graded rather than a sharp lock.
There was no clear difference between 3-<5 and 5-<7 year olds for moderate amblyopia, so responsiveness is not a simple monotone function of age within the early window.

The pooled analysis compares ages across treatments; it does not isolate penalisation magnitude as a variable, so the magnitude half of the analogy is carried by the clinical logic of the treatments rather than tested dose-response.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Individual-subject meta-analysis of four PEDIG randomized amblyopia treatment trials (children 3 to <13 years, unilateral amblyopia 20/40 to 20/400), adjusted for baseline acuity, refractive error, amblyopia type, prior treatment, study treatment and protocol. Children 7 to <13 years were significantly less responsive to treatment than children 3 to <5 or 5 to <7 for moderate and severe amblyopia; amblyopia is more responsive to treatment below age 7, although some older children show a marked response.
mapping.ree_translation: Amblyopia is the clinical form of competitive capture: one eye wins cortical territory and the other is under-represented. The standard treatments penalise the dominant (fellow) eye so the weaker eye's pathway can gain weight, and this trial shows the effect is strongest in the early window. That is the ARC-075 recipe at the level of human circuitry -- asymmetric magnitude suppression of the winner, timed to the plasticity-open window -- and it also illustrates what happens without the asymmetry: the developmental window passes and the imbalance persists.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Ocular dominance is competition between sensory input channels for cortical representation; ARC-075 concerns competition between a scoring pathway (F) and diversity circuits for control of action selection. The analogy is at the level of 'suppress the winner inside a window', not at the level of mechanism. The meta-analysis pools different treatment protocols and does not manipulate penalisation strength, and the age effect is graded (older responders exist), so it cannot support a sharp one-time lock.
mapping.source_context: Paediatric ophthalmology; pooled individual-patient data from four multicentre randomized controlled trials (Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group), human children 3-13 years.

confidence_components.notes: RCT-derived human data with careful covariate adjustment. Mapping is an explicit analogy from sensory-channel competition to scorer competition, so fidelity is moderate; the graded age effect is itself informative for the closure-trigger design.
